c.tagline: Year-round spring on an Atlantic city beach, with a colonial old town at its back.

taxi.fareNote: Official taxis are white with a green roof-light when free; fares are metered with a fixed supplement from the airport. Uber is not available in the city — Cabify operates on the island alongside regular taxis.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU-style emergency number for police, fire and ambulance across Spain.

hood_landmark.Vegueta (Old Town): Vegueta, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria
hood_landmark.Triana: Calle Triana, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria
hood_landmark.Santa Catalina / Puerto: Parque de Santa Catalina, Las Palmas
hood_landmark.Las Canteras: Playa de Las Canteras, Las Palmas

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing on Las Canteras beach and in the centre

hood_desc: The cobbled 15th-century old town where the city began — Santa Ana Cathedral, the Columbus House museum and Plaza de Santa Ana anchor a maze of colonial mansions, tapas bars and Sunday markets; the atmospheric first-timer base for history.
A lively pedestrian shopping street of modernist facades linking the old town to the port, full of boutiques, cafes and the Pérez Galdós theatre; central and walkable, good for shoppers.
The port and Santa Catalina Park district near the cruise terminal and El Muelle mall, buzzing with bars, restaurants and the city's liveliest nightlife; convenient for arrivals and going out.
The golden 3km city beach backed by a car-free promenade of seafood terraces and surf shops, sheltered by a natural reef; the sun-and-sand base most visitors choose.
A leafy, upscale residential quarter around Doramas Park and the historic Santa Catalina hotel, minutes from Las Canteras but calmer and greener; suits those wanting quiet with easy beach access.
lodging: Santa Catalina, a Royal Hideaway Hotel

water.note: Tap water is safe though desalinated; many prefer bottled for taste.

transit.pay: Buses take cash, contactless bank cards or the rechargeable TransGC/Guaguas card; a single city ride is about €1.40. No metro or tram exists, though a MetroGuagua bus-rapid-transit line is being built.
transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6am to midnight, with a reduced night-bus (búho) network on the main corridors.
transit.note: Las Palmas relies entirely on buses: yellow Guaguas Municipales inside the city and green Global coaches to the rest of Gran Canaria. Taxis fill late-night gaps.

ferry: Puerto de Las Palmas (Muelle de Santa Catalina)

transit.m: Global express bus line 60 to Santa Catalina/San Telmo, ~30-40 min

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up or leaving small change / 5-10% for good service is appreciated.

food.name: Papas arrugadas con mojo
food.desc: Small potatoes boiled in heavily salted water until the skins wrinkle, served with green coriander mojo and red pepper mojo picon.

places.name: El Monje de Santa Ana
places.note: Canarian home cooking on a terrace facing the cathedral; strong on the classics.

places.name: Mercado del Puerto
places.note: Iron-framed market with tapas counters doing papas and mojo all day.

places.name: La Tasca de Mawa
places.note: Busy neighbourhood tasca for octopus, seafood stew and Canarian sides.

food.name: Ropa vieja canaria
food.desc: Shredded beef and chickpeas stewed with potato, onion and pepper. The island version often uses chicken too and comes with fried potatoes.

places.name: El Monje de Santa Ana
places.note: Recipes handed down from Canarian grandmothers; ropa vieja is a fixture.

places.name: Casa Montesdeoca
places.note: Historic courtyard house serving traditional island dishes in a 16th-century patio.

places.name: Mercado de Vegueta
places.note: Century-old market whose bar counters cook guisos at lunchtime.

food.name: Escaldon de gofio
food.desc: Toasted grain flour scalded with hot fish or meat broth into a thick porridge, eaten with a spoon carved from onion. The oldest Canarian staple.

places.name: Casa Montesdeoca
places.note: Traditional kitchen that still puts gofio on the menu, not just in dessert.

places.name: Mercado del Puerto
places.note: Stalls sell gofio by weight and the bars serve escaldon as a tapa.

places.name: El Monje de Santa Ana
places.note: Good place to try gofio alongside other Canarian country dishes.

food.name: Sancocho canario
food.desc: Salted cherne or corvina desalted and poached with sweet potato and papas, served with mojo and a ball of gofio. Traditionally a Friday dish.

places.name: La Marinera
places.note: Seafront classic for island fish cooking with sunset views over the bay.

places.name: Allende Muelle
places.note: Harbourside kitchen built around fish, langoustines and salt cod.

places.name: Mercado de Vegueta
places.note: Fish counters sell salted cherne and nearby bars cook the dish at weekends.

food.name: Queso asado con mojo
food.desc: Slabs of fresh Canarian goat cheese grilled until they blister, served with mojo or a drizzle of palm honey. Also breaded as queso frito.

places.name: Mercado del Puerto
places.note: Cheese stalls and tapas bars side by side; try flor de Guia when available.

places.name: El Monje de Santa Ana
places.note: Serves island cheeses grilled with mojo as a starter on the cathedral terrace.

places.name: La Tasca de Mawa
places.note: Casual tasca where grilled cheese sits well next to a cold Tropical.

food.name: Bienmesabe
food.desc: Thick almond, egg yolk and lemon cream from Tejeda, spooned over ice cream or eaten straight. Sweet, dense and unmistakably Canarian.

places.name: Mercado de Vegueta
places.note: Stalls sell jars of Tejeda bienmesabe and other island preserves.

places.name: Casa Montesdeoca
places.note: Traditional Canarian desserts served in the historic patio.

places.name: Mercado del Puerto
places.note: Sweet counters carry bienmesabe, frangollo and palm honey.

food.name: Barraquito
food.desc: Layered Canarian coffee: condensed milk, Licor 43, espresso, foamed milk, lemon peel and cinnamon. Ask for it sin alcohol to skip the liqueur.

places.name: Mercado de Vegueta
places.note: Market cafeterias pull them properly layered for traders all morning.

places.name: Mercado del Puerto
places.note: Coffee counters inside the market are a good mid-shopping stop.

places.name: Calle Triana cafes
places.note: Pedestrian street lined with terraces serving barraquitos from breakfast on.

food.name: Tropical beer
food.desc: The pale lager brewed in Las Palmas since 1924 and poured everywhere as a small, very cold cana. Ron miel from Arucas is the local nightcap.

places.name: Mercado del Puerto
places.note: Market tapas bars pour it all day; the classic setting for a cana and a pincho.

places.name: La Tasca de Mawa
places.note: Local bar within earshot of the surf, good for beer with seafood tapas.

places.name: Paseo de Las Canteras terraces
places.note: Beachfront terraces along the promenade for a sunset cana.

landmarks: Playa de Las Canteras
One of the world's great urban beaches, three kilometers of golden sand sheltered by a natural offshore reef and backed by a lively promenade.
Vegueta Old Town
The city's 15th-century foundational quarter, a UNESCO-candidate grid of cobbled lanes, wooden balconies and plazas where Castile first anchored in the Atlantic.
Catedral de Santa Ana
The Canaries' mother cathedral, five centuries in the making, whose twin bell towers and rooftop terrace overlook Vegueta's finest square.
Casa de Colón
A gorgeously balconied colonial palace museum where Columbus reputedly stopped in 1492, tracing the islands' pivotal role in Atlantic exploration.
Museo Canario
The essential museum of pre-Hispanic Gran Canaria, famed for its hall of aboriginal Guanche skulls, mummies and painted idols like the Ídolo de Tara.
Auditorio Alfredo Kraus
A fortress-like concert hall by Óscar Tusquets rising from the surf at Las Canteras' southern end, its window framing the ocean behind the stage.
Castillo de la Luz
The city's oldest fortress, a 15th-century harbor castle that repelled Drake's raiders, now an art foundation devoted to sculptor Martín Chirino.
Calle Mayor de Triana
The elegant pedestrian shopping street of the Triana quarter, lined with modernist facades, century-old shops and buzzing cafe terraces.
Parque Santa Catalina
The port district's palm-filled plaza, home to the Elder Science Museum, carnival celebrations and the city's most cosmopolitan street life.
Jardín Botánico Canario Viera y Clavijo
Spain's largest botanical garden, terraced into the Guiniguada ravine and devoted to dragon trees, cardones and the Canaries' unique endemic flora.

train.note: The Canary Islands have no railways; a light-rail line for Gran Canaria has long been proposed but not built.

bus.note: No international buses. Green Global coaches run island-wide across Gran Canaria from the Santa Catalina and San Telmo interchanges, reaching the south resorts, mountain villages and the airport.

ferry.note: Fred. Olsen Express and Naviera Armas/Trasmediterránea sail from the Port of Las Palmas to Tenerife, Fuerteventura and Lanzarote, plus a long mainland crossing to Huelva/Cádiz.

half.name: Maspalomas Dunes
half.blurb: Sahara-like sand dunes and a lighthouse beach on the sunny south coast, about an hour away.

half.name: Teror
half.blurb: A pretty mountain town of carved wooden balconies and the island's Virgen del Pino basilica.

full.name: Roque Nublo & Tejeda
full.blurb: A drive into the volcanic caldera to the iconic Roque Nublo monolith and the whitewashed village of Tejeda.

full.name: Puerto de Mogán
full.blurb: A canal-laced fishing village known as 'Little Venice' on the southwest coast.
